motion-2d-s1.title: A ball rolls off a table
motion-2d-s1.text: A ball rolls off the edge of a level table 0.80 m high at 2.4 m/s, moving horizontally. Air resistance is negligible. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
motion-2d-s1.html: Key: gold arrow, the ball's velocity as it leaves the table; dashed curve, its path.

motion-2d-s2.title: Video tracking of a kicked ball
motion-2d-s2.text: A soccer ball is kicked from level ground at 18.0 m/s, 37.0° above the horizontal. A video tracker records its position. Air resistance is negligible; g = 9.8 m/s².

table.caption: Position of the ball after the kick

motion-2d-s3.title: A drone drops a package
motion-2d-s3.text: A delivery drone flies horizontally at a steady 6.0 m/s, 20. m above level ground, and releases a package. Air resistance is negligible. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
motion-2d-s3.html: Key: gold arrow, the drone's velocity relative to the ground.

items.q: How long is the ball in the air?

mistakes.why: Value: 0.33 s divides the height by the horizontal speed. The fall time comes from the vertical motion alone: Δy = ½gt².
Value: you forgot the square root: t² = 2Δy/g, so t = √(2Δy/g).

why.correct: Vertically the ball starts with v<sub>y</sub> = 0 and falls 0.80 m: Δy = ½gt², so t = √(2Δy/g) = √(2 × 0.80 m ÷ 9.8 m/s²) = 0.40 s. The horizontal speed does not matter.

items.q: How far from the base of the table does the ball land (the distance d)?

mistakes.why: Value: there is no ½ in the horizontal motion. With no horizontal acceleration, d = vₓt.
Value: use the fall time from the vertical motion, 0.40 s, not 0.80 m ÷ 2.4 m/s.

why.correct: Horizontally there is no acceleration, so d = vₓt = (2.4 m/s)(0.404 s) = 0.97 m.

items.q: The ball leaves the same table at 4.8 m/s instead. How does its time in the air compare?
options: It is twice as long
It is half as long
It is √2 times as long
It is the same, 0.40 s

why.correct: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Same height, same vertical start, same fall time; only d doubles.
options: A faster horizontal speed carries the ball farther, but it does not change how long it takes to fall 0.80 m.
The vertical motion starts from v<sub>y</sub> = 0 in both cases, so the ball falls the same way.
Square roots come from changing the height; here only the horizontal speed changed.
Right: the fall time depends only on the vertical motion (height and g), and the vertical motion has not changed.

items.q: What is the ball's speed just before it hits the floor?

mistakes.why: Value: 6.4 m/s adds the components as numbers. They are perpendicular, so combine them with the Pythagorean theorem.
Value: 4.0 m/s is only the vertical component. The ball still moves sideways at 2.4 m/s.

why.correct: vₓ = 2.4 m/s (unchanged). v<sub>y</sub> = gt = (9.8 m/s²)(0.404 s) = 3.96 m/s downward. Speed = √(2.4² + 3.96²) = 4.6 m/s.

items.q: Which statement about the ball's velocity while it is in the air is correct?
options: Its horizontal component slows down as the ball falls
Its horizontal part is steady; its vertical part grows
Both components grow at the same rate
Its vertical component stays zero until it lands

why.correct: A projectile: aₓ = 0, so vₓ is constant; a_y = −g, so v<sub>y</sub> grows downward steadily.
options: Nothing pushes the ball sideways once it leaves the table, so vₓ does not change.
Right: no horizontal acceleration; a constant downward acceleration g changes v<sub>y</sub> by 9.8 m/s each second.
Only the vertical component changes; the horizontal acceleration is zero.
Gravity gives the ball a downward velocity from the moment it leaves the table.

items.q: Using the table, what is the ball's horizontal velocity?

mistakes.why: Value: 18.0 m/s is the launch speed along the 37° direction. Only its horizontal component, v cos θ, shows up in x.
Value: 10.8 m/s is the vertical component, v sin θ.

why.correct: x grows by the same amount in equal times: from 0.00 s to 2.00 s, Δx = 28.75 m, so vₓ = 28.75 m ÷ 2.00 s = 14.4 m/s. Check: 18.0 cos 37.0° = 14.4 m/s.

items.q: At what time does the ball reach its highest point?

mistakes.why: Value: 2.21 s is the whole flight. The top comes halfway, when v<sub>y</sub> = 0.
Value: use the vertical component, 18.0 sin 37.0° = 10.8 m/s, not the full launch speed.

why.correct: At the top, v<sub>y</sub> = 0. v<sub>y</sub> = v₀ sin θ − gt → t = (18.0 sin 37.0°) ÷ 9.8 = 10.83 ÷ 9.8 = 1.11 s. The table agrees: the height peaks near 1.10 s.

items.q: Which describes a graph of the ball's vertical velocity v<sub>y</sub> against time (up positive)?
options: A horizontal line at 14.4 m/s
A curve that rises and then falls, like the path of the ball
A straight line sloping down, crossing zero near 1.1 s
A straight line sloping down that stops at zero

why.correct: Vertical motion: constant acceleration −g. v<sub>y</sub> starts at +10.8 m/s and falls by 9.8 m/s each second, through zero at about 1.1 s.
options: That describes vₓ, which does not change.
That shape is y against t. The velocity changes steadily, so its graph is straight.
Right: v<sub>y</sub> changes at a constant −9.8 m/s², so the graph is a line with slope −9.8 m/s², zero at the top.
After the top, v<sub>y</sub> keeps decreasing and becomes negative as the ball falls.

items.q: Where does the ball land, measured horizontally from the kick?

mistakes.why: Value: 15.9 m is where the ball is at its highest point. On level ground the flight takes twice as long.
Value: use the horizontal component of the velocity, 14.4 m/s, not 18.0 m/s.

why.correct: The flight lasts 2 × 1.105 s = 2.21 s (up and down on level ground). Range = vₓ × t = 14.38 m/s × 2.21 s = 31.8 m.

items.q: The ball is kicked again at 18.0 m/s but at 53.0° (so sin and cos swap). How do the new range and time of flight compare with the 37.0° kick?
options: The same range, but a longer time of flight
A longer range and a longer time of flight
A shorter range and the same time of flight
The same range and the same time of flight

why.correct: Time of flight = 2v sin θ/g grows with θ. Range = vₓ × time = 2v² sin θ cos θ/g, and sin θ cos θ is the same for 37° and 53°.
options: Right: range ∝ sin θ cos θ, which is the same for 37° and 53°; the larger vertical component keeps the ball up longer.
The longer flight is offset by a smaller horizontal velocity; the product, the range, is the same.
The time of flight depends on v sin θ, which is larger at 53°.
The ranges match, but at 53° the ball goes higher and stays up longer.

items.q: How long does the package take to reach the ground?

mistakes.why: Value: take the square root: t² = 2Δy/g = 4.08 s², so t = 2.0 s.
Value: the fall time comes from the vertical motion alone, not from 20 m ÷ 6.0 m/s.

why.correct: At release the package moves with the drone: horizontally at 6.0 m/s, vertically at 0. Δy = ½gt² → t = √(2 × 20. m ÷ 9.8 m/s²) = 2.0 s.

items.q: How far ahead of the target should the drone release the package, measured horizontally?

mistakes.why: Value: released straight above the target, the package would land 12 m past it: it keeps moving forward at 6.0 m/s.
Value: there is no ½ in the horizontal motion, since aₓ = 0.

why.correct: The package keeps the drone's horizontal velocity: d = vₓt = (6.0 m/s)(2.02 s) = 12 m before the target.

items.q: Where is the package relative to the drone while it falls, if the drone keeps flying at 6.0 m/s?
options: Behind the drone, falling farther back each second
Directly below the drone the whole time
Ahead of the drone, pulling farther in front of it
At the drone's height, moving sideways

why.correct: In the drone's frame the package has zero horizontal velocity and falls straight down. In the ground's frame the same motion is a curved path.
options: That would happen with air resistance slowing the package; here it keeps vₓ = 6.0 m/s.
Right: both have the same horizontal velocity, so relative to the drone the package just falls straight down.
Nothing speeds the package up horizontally.
Gravity pulls the package down from the moment it is released.

items.q: Which describes the package's path as seen by a person standing on the ground?
options: A downward curve that gets steeper
A straight line down
A straight slanted line toward the target
A curve that rises first, then falls

why.correct: Ground frame: x = vₓt and y = −½gt². Combining them gives a parabola that gets steeper as v<sub>y</sub> grows.
options: Right: steady horizontal motion plus growing downward speed traces a downward-curving path, a parabola.
That is the path in the drone's frame. On the ground, the package also moves forward at 6.0 m/s.
A straight slanted path would need a constant ratio of v<sub>y</sub> to vₓ, but v<sub>y</sub> grows while vₓ stays the same.
The package is released with no upward velocity, so it never rises.

items.q: At the highest point of a ball's flight after being thrown at an angle, which is true? Air resistance is negligible.
options: Its velocity and acceleration are both zero
Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is g downward
Its velocity is horizontal and its acceleration is zero
Its velocity is horizontal; its acceleration is g down

why.correct: At the top v<sub>y</sub> = 0 but vₓ is unchanged, and a = g downward at every point of a projectile's flight.
options: vₓ is not zero, and the acceleration stays g downward at the top.
Only the vertical part of the velocity is zero at the top; vₓ remains.
The vertical velocity is changing from up to down at the top, so the acceleration is not zero.
Right: v<sub>y</sub> = 0 at the top, so the velocity is just vₓ; the acceleration is g down throughout.

items.q: Two balls roll off the edges of two tables at the same horizontal speed. Table B is 4.0 times as high as table A. Ball A lands 0.50 m from its table. How far from its table does ball B land?

mistakes.why: Value: 2.0 m assumes d ∝ h. The fall time grows as √h, so d grows by √4 = 2.
Value: d grows as √h, not h².

why.correct: Fall time t = √(2h/g) ∝ √h, so B falls √4.0 = 2.0 times as long. With the same vₓ, d = vₓt doubles: 1.0 m.

items.q: A ball is launched at 25 m/s, 60.° above the horizontal. What is the vertical component of its initial velocity? (Degree mode.)

mistakes.why: Value: 13 m/s is the horizontal component. The vertical side is opposite the angle from the ground: use sine.

why.correct: v<sub>y</sub> = v sin θ = (25 m/s) sin 60.° = 22 m/s.
